Benchmarking

4 min read
Just now

--

The score everyone quotes to prove an agent is smart is the number you should trust the least. A field note from the 2026 evaluation crisis.
Every time a new AI agent launches, it arrives holding a number. “80% on SWE-bench.” “State of the art on GAIA.” The number does the persuading. We read it, update our beliefs about what the model can do, and move on.
I spend a lot of my time building and running evaluations for AI agents, and here is what that work has taught me: the number is the least trustworthy part of the announcement. Not because people are lying, but because the benchmark underneath it is quietly broken in ways a single score hides. In 2026 this stopped being a niche complaint and became the field’s biggest problem.
The scores are saturating, and worse
Take the headline benchmark for coding agents, SWE-bench. Two things happened this year that should have been bigger news than any model release. First, saturation: progress on SWE-bench Verified slowed from roughly 75% to 81% over six months, and when everyone is bunched near the ceiling, the gaps between models stop being signal and start being noise. Second, and more damning: OpenAI audited a set of the hard tasks and reported that a majority, around 59% of the ones examined, had material problems in the tests or the task design. The benchmark used to crown coding agents was itself substantially broken.
This is not one bad benchmark. Across the board, evaluation is buckling under contamination, gaming, and annotation error rates reported above 50%. The leaderboard number, the thing we treat as ground truth, is often measuring something other than the ability it claims to.
What the score is actually made of
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Only one of these is real capability. The other three are measurement artifacts.
• Contamination: the model has seen the answers. Test sets leak into training data. A high score can mean strong memorization, not capability. It is testing the open-book student on the exact questions they studied, then calling them a genius.

• Broken tasks and graders: the benchmark is wrong. Early WebArena failed an agent that answered “$1200” instead of “1200 USD” despite it being correct. Multiply rigid grading across thousands of tasks and the score reflects how well the model matched the grader’s quirks, not whether it did the job.

• Gaming and overfitting: Goodhart’s law. When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. Once a benchmark is the thing everyone competes on, the score rises without the underlying ability moving.

• Saturation: no signal left. When top models all sit at 80-something percent, the remaining gaps are often inside the noise of the benchmark’s own errors. Ranking by that gap measures the ruler’s defects.
Only one of these is the model genuinely being good. The rest are artifacts of how we measured. The single number tells you none of the mixture.
The trap, again
If you have read my other writing, you know the shape of this. My models once beat their baseline while being worse than a coin flip, because I read a relative metric and never checked calibration. A RAG system produces a fluent, cited answer that is completely wrong, because fluency is not truth. And now an agent posts a record benchmark score while being no more capable than last year’s. Every time, the failure wears the costume of success. The number goes up, the demo works, the answer sounds right, and the only defense is refusing to trust a good-looking result until you have checked what it is made of.
How to read a benchmark like it might be lying
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Real capability is consistent across evals. An artifact only shows up in one place.Triangulate. Never trust one number. Look across several benchmarks, harnesses, and model versions. Real capability shows up consistently; artifacts do not.
Check for contamination. Ask whether the test set could be in the training data. A held-out or freshly built evaluation is worth ten public leaderboards.
Audit the tasks and the grader, not just the score. Read what “pass” actually means. In 2026, those checks are frequently wrong.
Prefer dynamic, workflow-realistic evals. Static public sets are the easiest to contaminate and game.
Measure the reasons, not the outcome. A right answer reached by a broken path is not capability, the same way a matching score reached through contamination is not progress.
The takeaway
A benchmark score is a hypothesis about capability. It is not proof, and in 2026 it is often not even good evidence. The field spent years treating leaderboard numbers as ground truth, and we are now discovering how much of that ground was contamination, broken graders, and Goodharted targets.
The uncomfortable part is that none of this looks like a problem from the outside. The score is high, the chart goes up and to the right, and most people never dig. I have stopped asking what a model scored. I ask what that score is made of, and whether it would survive being measured a different way. Because the lesson keeps repeating, in metrics, in RAG, and now in benchmarks: looking right is not the same as being right, and telling the difference is the whole job.
What is a benchmark number you have seen quoted as proof that turned out to be hollow? I collect these.
